questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Academically, I knew that Korea - and especially Korea University, as it is part of SKY (the top universities in Korea) - was well regarded, so I did not have to worry about the level of education. However, the main driving force behind choosing Korea was my interest in the country and its culture. I wanted to try living in a country that was very different from Denmark, so I looked toward Asia. I ultimately chose Korea because it felt more “Western” than many other Asian countries, which I believed would make it easier to adapt.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy. Korea University was very thorough in their emails and provided a lot of information, which significantly reduced my concerns about not knowing what to do. Before arrival, they shared detailed information about both on-campus and off-campus housing to help students get started with their search. They also provided clear information about when and where to meet on orientation day before the semester started. Since I chose on-campus housing, I also received detailed instructions on how to travel from the airport to campus, which made the arrival process very straightforward.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There is an orientation day where you meet fellow exchange students as well as your buddies. Buddies are local students who are part of a program called KUBA, and their role is to help exchange students with any questions they may have. Each exchange student is assigned one buddy before orientation day and the start of the semester, and the buddies also arrange group meetings and dinners throughout the semester. If you have questions, you can either contact the Global Service Center at Korea University or reach out to your buddy.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The only thing you really had to do was apply for your first and second priorities among single and double rooms. The rest is handled by them, and you’ll be assigned a room before you arrive.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There is a kitchen where you can cook, but I didn’t use it. In general, it’s cheaper to buy food than to cook it yourself, so it also depends on whether you prefer cooking or not. However, right next to the dormitories, there is a cafeteria that is very affordable, and the food is generally good. Breakfast costs 1,000 KRW (5 DKK), while lunch and dinner cost 6,000 KRW (30 DKK). The cafeteria is open on weekdays, and it’s important to note that there is no curfew for the dorms!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
The on-campus housing is very affordable and has overall good facilities. I lived at Anam International House, and it was a very positive experience. I had a good roommate, which is extremely important for the quality of the stay, and I encountered very few problems during my time there. Every day, there is an RA (a senior student who lives in the dormitory) in the lobby from 8 p.m. to 12 a.m., who can help if you have any problems or questions. Otherwise, you can visit the nearby office for assistance.

When applying for housing, it is first come, first served, so you have to be prepared. For me, the application opened at 3 a.m., and the website crashed and lagged due to heavy traffic. Because there is a queue system, I was not finished until 6 a.m. You simply have to be patient during the process.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The process initially seems very intimidating because there are many required documents and several strict deadlines. However, both Korea University and KU in Denmark are very good at providing detailed emails explaining exactly which documents are needed, what to submit, and where to send them. If you gather the documents and follow the instructions as soon as you receive the emails, the process is not overly stressful and is very manageable. Therefore, the administrative work should not discourage you from applying.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They always provided a contact person or a department email address that you could write to if you had questions. In most cases, you would receive a response within a few working days.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I applied for preapproval for 10 courses (5 courses = 30 ECTS) so that I would have multiple options when registering. However, 6 out of the 10 courses were not offered that semester, as the preapproval was based on the previous semester’s course list. As a result, I had to apply for new preapprovals quickly.
Course registration at the host university operates on a first-come, first-served basis, and registration opens according to Korean time. This meant I had to be ready at 3 a.m. Danish time to apply. Depending on how popular the courses are, they can fill up within seconds or minutes, so it is very important to be prepared. Fortunately, I managed to get all five courses I applied for.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They provide clear information and detailed descriptions of the required documents and deadlines, so my advice is to complete each task as soon as you receive the email. This gives you plenty of time to handle any unforeseen delays. It is also easy to get in contact with both KU and Korea University if you have questions. Most importantly, make sure to keep all deadlines - you may lose your spot otherwise.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: For the courses I took, which were mostly media-related, the academic level was quite similar to that at KU. One notable difference is that Korean universities use midterm and final exams, and the exams are often multiple-choice, true/false, or fill-in-the-blank. Therefore, this might make the examination format somewhat different, depending on your major.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching style was very similar. Some classes were lecture-based, where you primarily listen, while others required active participation and usually at least one presentation during the semester. All of my presentations were group-based and very similar to those at KU, so there was nothing unfamiliar.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend INTRODUCTION TO MEDIA and UNDERSTANDING SOCIAL MEDIA. Both courses were well structured, and I really liked the professors, who were very kind and engaging. Introduction to Media is a lecture-based course where the midterm and final assessments consist of two assignments rather than exams. Understanding Social Media is more interactive and discussion-based, but the professor is very welcoming, which creates a comfortable learning environment. Both courses provide valuable insights into media on a global scale and its societal impact.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It wasn't unexpected for me but a nice to know anyway. You have to pay a mandatory national health insurance which is about 77.300 KRW (364 DKK) every month. You will get more information about what it is and how to pay when you arrive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Generally everything is cheaper in Korea - food, drinks, clothes, electronics, etc. So I chose to not bring that much clothing and then buy while I was here. For food you can cook yourself, but you won’t save much, if any, compared to eating out. Of course, depending on where you eat as well - some restaurants are way cheaper than others, e.g., Korean restaurants are quite cheap where you can get a big meal for 10.000 KRW (50 DKK), other places like western, especially if also popular, can cost around 22.000 - 30.000 KRW (110 - 132 DKK).
Something that surprised me a lot was that fruit is really expensive. It costs more than in Denmark, so be prepared to either spend some money on fruit or live without.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are all sorts of activities and we also got information about which clubs we could apply for. I do know some clubs can be difficult to enter if you don’t speak Korean. However, I know some exchange students that joined a football club and went to matches against other schools. But I didn’t apply to any.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I mean it really depends on what you like. Like I said, I didn’t apply to anything so I can’t really tell how the process is. But if you like hiking, Seoul is a very good place to be - it is located next to mountains, so there are some good trails and also just walking in the city you can come across some very steep hills.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: A lot of people use the time to travel outside of Seoul to see more of Korea - mostly Busan or Jeju are really popular places to visit. Although Chuseok, which is a national holiday in Korea where you get almost 1 week off, is very popular to travel and therefore it is way more expensive than any other time. What a lot of people did was to choose courses that didn’t have class on Fridays, so they would get Friday off completely and then spend the weekends traveling.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It entirely depends on you and the mindset you bring with you. I did a lot of preparation and learned about the culture before I went, so the culture shock wasn’t that big for me - although there were still plenty of things and moments that surprised me. The most important thing is to be open-minded and respectful toward both the people and the culture. Koreans are generally very friendly, especially if you show genuine interest in the country and its culture and behave respectfully.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Early on I got myself a Korean girlfriend and almost all of my friends were locals, so I did a lot of socializing with local students. Regarding getting friends, we probably wouldn’t have become friends if I hadn’t taken the initiative to approach them and encourage them to meet up. That’s not something I would normally do in Denmark, but I felt it was necessary in order to get to know people. However, I think my curious mindset and friendly, respectful approach made it less difficult for me. 

There is still a language barrier, and not everyone feels comfortable speaking English, which can make things a bit challenging. That said, my encounters with people happened quite naturally. The main takeaway is that you generally have to be the one who takes the initiative.

Before I went, one of the things I did to learn as much as possible about the people and the culture was to download a language exchange app called Tandem. I don’t speak, write, or fully understand Korean, but I thought people might still be interested since many want to practice their English - and a lot of them were. They were eager to share information about their country and culture, and I received plenty of advice on what to do and not to do, what to see, eat, and experience in general.
So, if you’re interested in immersing yourself in the culture and making it easier to connect with people, I would definitely recommend trying that app or similar ones.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: As I’ve mentioned earlier, I did a lot of preparation and actively wanted to immerse myself in the culture, so there wasn’t anything specific that I found particularly challenging. Danish and Korean cultures are quite different, so what feels most challenging can vary greatly from person to person.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really like Korean culture, so it’s hard for me to single out just one aspect. However, if I had to choose something I find particularly influential, it would be that people are generally very polite and respectful, which makes you feel welcome and comfortable being there.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be kind and respectful - this is highly valued in Korea.
2. Be open and proactive when meeting people, even if that’s not something you would normally do. It will ultimately make your stay more fun and enjoyable. Remember, others are often in the same situation as you and want to meet new people too.
3. Stay in the moment and enjoy the experience. Time passes very quickly, so try to be present and make the most of it while it lasts.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Before you leave, you’ll probably need to have your photo taken at a photo store, as it’s required for your visa application. If possible, ask to receive a digital copy as well. When applying for your ARC (Alien Registration Card, which functions as your ID), you need to submit a digital photo.
In my case, I only had physical copies, so I had to find a photo store in Korea to get my picture taken again and obtain a digital version. It’s not a big issue, but if you can take care of it in advance, you might as well do so.
I applied for the ARC around the beginning of the semester.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting people from all over the world was extremely fun. Building meaningful relationships with people who are very different from you gives you so much to learn from, and it often leads to fun and memorable moments when cultures clash. Those experiences were probably my most cherished moments, along with forming genuine and meaningful connections with others in general.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Honestly, I’m not sure. My exchange went quite smoothly, so there weren’t any major issues. The few less-than-ideal situations I encountered were easily resolved without any significant consequences.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
